summary: Modifies the device-independent graphics display proposal in RFC 177. The main change is how coordinate areas on the network standard graphics screen are defined, to avoid a problem found with the earlier definition and to be more flexible.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC revises how the graphics proposal in RFC 177 defines areas and coordinates. It lets a list be placed and scaled within a specified image area and adds commands for saving and restoring display modes.

questions: how are graphics coordinate areas defined
what is the network standard graphics screen
what did rfc 181 change in rfc 177
what are the new graphics mode stack commands
subtitle: A revision to coordinate areas and scaling in the RFC 177 graphics proposal.

tldr.problem: In RFC 177, graphics lists could cross intended area boundaries, and scaling lists was awkward.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 181 defines coordinates as normalized fractions relative to an area or image space, and changes execute and copy list commands to specify two corners.
tldr.outcome: It also adds mode-stack commands and changes the definition of a list. The unit metadata says it updates RFC 177.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 181 as Unknown and says it updates RFC 177. No later RFC is listed as replacing it.

sections.title: Problems in the Earlier Proposal
sections.content: RFC 181 modifies the device-independent graphics proposal in RFC 177. The earlier area boundaries were meant to be absolute, but a list executed within an area could cross them. Scaling lists also relied on specific commands in the network graphic display list.
sections.plainLanguage: The earlier proposal could let a drawing cross its area's boundary. It also made resizing a list awkward.

sections.title: Areas and Relative Coordinates
sections.content:
Coordinates remain 16-bit unsigned normalized fractions, but are defined as fractional displacements from the lower-left corner of the screen, an area or an image space. The receiving device determines picture resolution.

Areas remain rectangular and may overlap, but one area may not completely contain another. Each area has a 16-bit integer name and lower-left and upper-right coordinate pairs relative to the network standard graphics screen. A list executed in an area may not cross that area's boundaries.
sections.plainLanguage: Coordinates are measured relative to the area where a list runs. The receiving display can map those fractions to its own screen resolution.

sections.title: List Scaling and Mode Stacks
sections.content:
List items 7 and 8 become EXECUTE LIST and COPY LIST commands with two coordinate pairs defining the image area. The pairs are relative to the containing area, so a list can be scaled differently each time it runs and can be distorted when the horizontal and vertical ratios differ.

Executing a list saves current state, computes a new origin, resets NGLP to zero and calculates new X and Y scale factors. Four new items push or pop character and vector modes: types 14 through 17.
sections.plainLanguage: Each execution can place a list in a chosen area and scale it for that area. New commands save and restore character and vector settings while lists run.

sections.title: Other Command Changes
sections.content:
DEFINE LIST now takes a 16-bit integer name and a 16-bit length measured in bytes rather than items. The RFC says this makes NGDS processing easier and eliminates the TABLE item, type 11.

The first three list items drop the words WORD IMAGE, and DEFINE IMAGE AREA becomes DEFINE AREA.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC changes some command names and the way list length is recorded. It also removes the TABLE item.

references.text: RFC 177, the device-independent graphical display description proposal modified by RFC 181.
